notes.heading: Overview
points: Citizenship determines full membership of the Indian political community
Only citizens enjoy certain rights like voting, holding constitutional posts, etc.
Part II of the Constitution deals with Citizenship (Articles 5 to 11)
The Constitution provides citizenship only at the commencement; later governed by Citizenship Act, 1955

notes.heading: Article 5 – Citizenship at Commencement
points: Person who had domicile in India and fulfilled conditions became citizen at commencement
Includes those born in India
Includes those who have at least one parent born in India
Includes those ordinarily resident in India for 5 years before commencement

notes.heading: Article 6 – Migrants from Pakistan to India
points: Deals with persons who migrated from Pakistan to India before 19 July 1948
Citizenship depends on residence and registration requirements
Special provisions for refugees during Partition
Simplified criteria for early migrants

notes.heading: Article 7 – Migrants to Pakistan and Returning
points: Persons who migrated to Pakistan after March 1, 1947 lost citizenship
However, those who returned under permit could regain citizenship
Ensured control over dual migration issues during Partition
Focused on post-Partition population movement

notes.heading: Article 8 – Persons of Indian Origin Abroad
points: Persons of Indian origin residing outside India could register as citizens
Must have parents or grandparents born in undivided India
Registration done by Indian diplomatic or consular representatives
Ensures connection with Indian diaspora

notes.heading: Article 9 – No Dual Citizenship
points: If a person voluntarily acquires citizenship of another country, Indian citizenship is lost
India does not allow dual citizenship in constitutional sense
Ensures single allegiance to one country
Later OCI (Overseas Citizen of India) is not full citizenship

notes.heading: Article 10 – Continuance of Citizenship
points: Every person who is or is deemed to be a citizen continues as citizen
Subject to any law made by Parliament
Citizenship can be regulated by legislation
Ensures stability of citizenship status

notes.heading: Article 11 – Parliament’s Power
points: Parliament has exclusive power to regulate citizenship
Includes acquisition and termination of citizenship
Basis for Citizenship Act, 1955
Constitution does not provide detailed citizenship rules

notes.heading: Citizenship Act, 1955 (Brief Idea)
points: Provides modes of acquiring citizenship: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory
Provides for termination and renunciation
Has been amended multiple times
Introduced OCI (Overseas Citizen of India) scheme

notes.heading: Important UPSC Points
points: No provision for dual citizenship in India
Articles 5–11 deal only with initial citizenship framework
Parliament has full power over citizenship laws
Citizenship is closely linked to Fundamental Rights

notes.heading: Overview
points: Citizenship refers to full and equal membership of a sovereign political state
It establishes a legal and political bond between an individual and the State
In India, citizenship is governed by Part II of the Constitution and Citizenship Act, 1955
Only citizens enjoy certain exclusive rights under the Constitution

notes.heading: Meaning of Citizenship
points: Citizenship is the status of being a legal member of a country
It includes rights, duties, and allegiance to the State
It distinguishes citizens from aliens (foreigners)
It ensures political identity within a nation-state

notes.heading: Citizens vs Aliens
points: Citizens enjoy full civil and political rights
Aliens do not enjoy political rights like voting or holding constitutional posts
Aliens are subject to restrictions under domestic law
Some Fundamental Rights are available to both citizens and non-citizens

notes.heading: Significance of Citizenship
points: Provides political rights such as voting and contesting elections
Ensures right to hold public offices like President, MP, MLA (with conditions)
Creates sense of belonging and national identity
Forms the basis of democratic participation

notes.heading: Constitutional Importance
points: Only citizens enjoy Fundamental Rights under Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30
Citizenship is essential for political rights like voting under Article 326
Ensures equality before law within the political community
Helps define the population of the sovereign state

notes.heading: Political Significance
points: Citizens participate in governance through elections
They can form and join political parties
They can influence policy-making and government formation
Citizenship ensures accountability of government

notes.heading: Legal Significance
points: Defines who is subject to full legal rights and obligations
Citizens cannot be arbitrarily deported
Ensures diplomatic protection from the State
Provides legal identity in domestic and international law

notes.heading: Citizenship in Indian Context
points: India follows single citizenship system
No state citizenship exists unlike federal countries like USA
Citizenship is uniform across all states and UTs
Ensures national unity and integration

notes.heading: Important UPSC Points
points: Citizenship is different from domicile
Only citizens enjoy full political rights
India has single citizenship system
Citizenship ensures both rights and duties in a democracy

notes.heading: Overview
points: The Citizenship Act, 1955 is the primary legislation governing Indian citizenship
It was enacted under Article 11 of the Constitution
It lays down provisions for acquisition and termination of citizenship after 26 January 1950
It has been amended multiple times to reflect changing national needs

notes.heading: Modes of Acquiring Citizenship
points: By Birth: A person born in India (subject to conditions in different periods of law)
By Descent: Citizenship through Indian parents
By Registration: For Persons of Indian Origin and certain categories of migrants
By Naturalisation: Citizenship granted after residing in India for a specified period and fulfilling conditions
By Incorporation of Territory: When new territory becomes part of India

notes.heading: Citizenship by Birth (Evolution)
points: Initially (1950–1987): Any person born in India was a citizen
1986 Amendment: At least one parent must be Indian citizen
2003 Amendment: One parent must be Indian citizen and other not an illegal migrant
Tighter rules introduced due to illegal migration concerns

notes.heading: Citizenship by Registration
points: Available to Persons of Indian Origin residing in India for a specified period
Spouses of Indian citizens can apply
Persons registered by Government of India
Helps in integrating diaspora and long-term residents

notes.heading: Citizenship by Naturalisation
points: Granted to foreigners who reside in India for 12 years (generally)
Requires good character and knowledge of Indian language
Must renounce previous citizenship (no dual citizenship)
Granted by Central Government discretion

notes.heading: Citizenship by Incorporation of Territory
points: When new territory becomes part of India, its residents become citizens
Example: Puducherry, Goa, Sikkim integration
Citizenship is automatically conferred by law
Ensures smooth political integration of new regions

notes.heading: Termination of Citizenship
points: Renunciation: Voluntary giving up of citizenship
Termination: Automatically when a person acquires foreign citizenship
Deprivation: Government can revoke citizenship in certain cases (fraud, disloyalty, etc.)
Ensures national security and legal compliance

notes.heading: Important Amendments
points: 1986 Amendment: Restricted citizenship by birth
2003 Amendment: Further tightened illegal migration provisions
2015 Amendment: Introduced Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) integration improvements
2019 Amendment (CAA): Fast-tracked citizenship for certain persecuted minorities from neighboring countries

notes.heading: Important UPSC Points
points: Citizenship Act is the operational law for citizenship in India
India does not permit dual citizenship
Parliament has full power to amend citizenship rules
Citizenship can be acquired in 5 different ways under the Act

notes.heading: Overview
points: India follows the system of Single Citizenship
Every citizen of India is a citizen of India only, not of any state separately
This is provided implicitly under the Constitution
It promotes unity and national integration

notes.heading: Meaning of Single Citizenship
points: A person has only one citizenship i.e., Indian citizenship
There is no separate citizenship for states like in federal countries such as the USA
All citizens enjoy uniform rights across the country
It removes the concept of state-based citizenship identity

notes.heading: Constitutional Basis
points: Articles 5–11 of the Constitution deal with citizenship framework
No provision for state citizenship exists in the Constitution
Citizenship Act, 1955 also provides only one national citizenship
India’s unitary bias in federal structure supports this system

notes.heading: Features of Single Citizenship
points: Uniform political and civil rights for all citizens
No discrimination between citizens based on state residence
Free movement and settlement across India
Equal eligibility for central government jobs

notes.heading: Comparison with Dual Citizenship Countries
points: Countries like USA, Australia have dual citizenship (national + state)
In India, no separate state citizenship exists
All citizens are treated equally across states
This strengthens national unity

notes.heading: Advantages of Single Citizenship
points: Promotes national integration and unity
Prevents regionalism and state-based discrimination
Ensures equal rights across the country
Strengthens integrity of the nation

notes.heading: Criticism of Single Citizenship
points: States have no separate identity in citizenship matters
May reduce importance of federal structure
Over-centralisation of identity at national level
Less scope for state-level political autonomy

notes.heading: Important Constitutional Support
points: Single Constitution for Union and States
Single Judiciary system
All India Services recruitment system
Fundamental Rights apply uniformly across states

notes.heading: Important UPSC Points
points: India follows single citizenship unlike USA
No state citizenship exists in India
Promotes unity and integrity of nation
It is a key feature of Indian Constitution’s unitary bias

notes.heading: Overview
points: OCI is a special status granted to Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs) living abroad
It was introduced through the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2005
OCI is NOT full citizenship of India
It provides certain lifelong visa and economic benefits

notes.heading: Background and Purpose
points: Created to strengthen emotional and economic ties with Indian diaspora
Demand arose from Indian-origin people in developed countries
Aimed at allowing easier travel and residence in India
Does not revive dual citizenship in constitutional sense

notes.heading: Eligibility for OCI
points: A foreign citizen who was eligible to become Indian citizen on 26 January 1950 or thereafter
Persons belonging to territories that became part of India after 15 August 1947
Children or grandchildren of such persons are eligible
Spouses of OCI cardholders (subject to conditions)

notes.heading: Rights Granted under OCI
points: Multiple entry, lifelong visa to India
Exemption from registration with Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO)
Parity with Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) in economic, financial, and educational fields (with restrictions)
Permission to own property (except agricultural land, unless specifically allowed)

notes.heading: Restrictions on OCI
points: No voting rights in India
Cannot hold constitutional posts like President, MP, or MLA
Cannot buy agricultural or plantation land
Not eligible for government employment

notes.heading: Legal Status of OCI
points: OCI is NOT Indian citizenship
It is a form of long-term visa with privileges
OCI cardholders remain foreign citizens
Does not provide political rights in India

notes.heading: Difference between OCI and Citizenship
points: Citizenship gives full political rights; OCI does not
Citizenship allows voting; OCI does not
Citizenship requires allegiance only to India; OCI holders are foreign citizens
OCI is revocable; citizenship is governed by stricter provisions

notes.heading: Important Amendments
points: OCI scheme introduced in 2005 amendment
Later amendments expanded eligibility conditions
2015 amendment merged PIO scheme with OCI
Rules have been periodically updated for simplification

notes.heading: Important UPSC Points
points: OCI is NOT dual citizenship
OCI is a lifelong visa with limited rights
It is governed by Citizenship Act, 1955 (amended)
It strengthens India’s global diaspora connection
